WASHINGTON, Oct 8 : More than 120 US lawmakers raised concerns on Thursday about Alphabet's Google unit acquiring defunct carrier Spirit Airlines' internal data for $10 million to train artificial intelligence systems. The lawmakers led by Senator Elizabeth Warren and Representative Steven Horsford said the sale would include 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams messages and other employee records. The lawmakers asked the company to "exclude employee information from the transaction to the greatest extent possible."

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Oct 8 : The four leaders of US President Donald Trump's AI task force are slated to meet on Thursday, task force vice chair Scott Kupor told Reuters, adding that he expects the full committee to convene next week as pressure builds on Washington to take action on AI. The task force is expected to help shape the administration's approach to AI at a pivotal moment for the technology.  Public uneasiness with AI, and the small group of people who seemingly hold sway over it, has risen in recent months. Most US voters think Trump's administration and Congress are not taking the risks of AI seriously enough and want the government to write new regulations for the technology, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Wednesday.  The AI companies "need to step up and demonstrate that they are taking concerns that people have around security and vulnerabilities very seriously, as do we," Kupor said.

Kupor said he expects the group to release a charter outlining its goals and responsibilities after its first full committee meeting. The group will have four to five staff members who will be assigned to the committee full-time, he said. Trump has dubbed the group the Super Intelligence Task Force, using his preferred term for artificial intelligence. It is led by Intelligence Director Jay Clayton, with Kupor, Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Defense Department technology lead Emil Michael. Trump calls the Defense Department the Department of War. Kupor said he will focus on engaging industries outside the technology sector, including banking, healthcare and utilities, to better understand how AI could affect their exposure to cyber threats. Michael will work directly with AI developers, Kupor said.

Source: Reuters

Oct 8 : Revolut would favor a primary listing in the United States if the digital bank decides to pursue an initial pubic offering in the future, CEO Nik Storonsky told Bloomberg TV on Thursday. Storonsky, who founded Revolut, told Bloomberg TV that the firm wants to "dominate" the US market and plans to roll out credit cards and loans, once it receives a full banking charter. Revolut received preliminary approval for a national banking licence in the United States in September, after getting licences in Britain and France earlier this year. The bank has risen to become Europe's most valuable startup, having grown rapidly since it was launched just over a decade ago as a fintech promising cheaper forex fees. Valued at $115 billion privately, Revolut is now worth more than Britain's Barclays  and France's Societe Generale. The company's top boss had previously told French newspaper Les Echos the bank was looking into a dual stock market listing in New York and London. Any eventual listing is still likely to be at least a year away, with past media reports citing 2028, and subject to market conditions.

Source: Reuters

MOSCOW, Oct 8 : Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Thursday it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data centre hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored. Yandex said earlier that the attack on its Sasovo hub, one of its five large data centres, caused a fire and forced it to suspend operations at the site, which hosts tens of thousands of servers. "The scale of the damage to the infrastructure is still being assessed," Yandex said in a statement. "For the moment, we cannot confirm whether it is possible to restore the data centre equipment in Sasovo." The company earlier said some of its services were unavailable and specialist teams were at the site assessing the damage. Two of Yandex's three supercomputers, used to develop its AI model, are housed at the Sasovo data centre. Yandex has not said whether they were damaged.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Oct 8 : President Donald Trump bought as much as $1.6 million and sold as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock in August, according to his latest financial disclosure, which was released on Thursday as he prepared to award Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang the nation's highest honor for scientific achievement. The new disclosure of the president's investment in one of the world's most valuable companies comes as his administration weighs policies that could shape Nvidia's fortunes, including rules governing exports of its advanced chips.  White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement to Reuters that third-party financial institutions independently manage the president's portfolio and replicate "recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000."  Huang is set to receive the National Medal of Science from Trump on Thursday. The award honors Americans who have made "outstanding contributions to knowledge in the physical, biological, mathematical, engineering, or social and behavioral sciences, in service to the nation," according to the National Science Foundation's website.

"There are no conflicts of interest.” Trump is also set to give the same award to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Google co-founder Sergey Brin on Thursday.  Nvidia's spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Oct 8 : Alphabet's Google Cloud on Thursday introduced the Gemini agent, a single AI agent for work that can answer questions, handle tasks, create content and write code. The move comes as tech companies race to sell AI that can work autonomously. The announcement comes after OpenAI's September launch of always-on agents called dots that chase user goals across apps on their own. Earlier last month, Meta released Muse, a personal AI agent that can shop, book travel, send emails and make payments for users. Alphabet shares were up marginally in early trading.

MADRID, Oct 8 : Spain's minority leftist government plans tighter oversight of future data centres ahead of an early parliamentary election set for November 29, Digital Transformation Minister Oscar Lopez said on Thursday. Spain is trying to balance data-centre investment from companies such as Amazon Web Services and Microsoft, mainly focussed in the northeastern region of Aragon, against concerns over the industry's consumption of energy and water and has drafted tougher water and electricity rules. Lopez said a decree regulating the fast-growing sector would not require parliamentary approval. "The government's intention is to move forward with that decree," Lopez told a conference on artificial intelligence, adding that ministries were still reviewing submissions from a public consultation and working on a common position. Amazon's AWS and Microsoft have said their plans in Aragon remain unaltered but both urged Spain to protect long-term investment by promoting legal certainty and predictability.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON: The Trump administration froze on Thursday (Oct 8) some green-card filings by Microsoft, Adobe and major IT outsourcers and opened probes into nine elite universities, widening a visa crackdown it says targets fraud and American job losses. The twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programmes, potentially blocking a common path to permanent residency for thousands of foreign tech workers while putting some of the country's most prominent research universities on notice. The moves come even as the administration cultivates closer ties with the same tech leaders whose companies are now in its crosshairs. "Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers," Vice President JD Vance said. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the suspension would also cover Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini.

"We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies," Sonderling said. Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for what the administration called the misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages. Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment. Under the Labour Department's permanent labour certification process, known as PERM, which is required for most employment-based green cards, employers must show that hiring a foreign worker will not harm the wages, working conditions or job opportunities of US workers. Approved applications then go to US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Related:

The freeze does not appear to directly affect current holders of H-1B visas, which allow companies to employ foreign workers temporarily. But it could block a common route by which employers sponsor those workers for permanent residency. Indian IT firms such as Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL, along with Cognizant, have long been among the biggest users of H-1B visas. Amazon.com was the largest employer of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2026, followed by Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Apple and Microsoft, according to USCIS data. Microsoft is also the largest filer of PERM applications, according to Permtrack.app, which compiles Labour Department disclosure data.

CRACKDOWN WIDENS The suspensions are the latest in a series of steps against skilled-worker programs. In September last year, the Labor Department launched an enforcement drive called "Project Firewall," as a White House proclamation imposed a one-time US$100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad. During President Donald Trump's second term, companies have faced growing pressure to keep jobs and production in the United States rather than move them overseas. The action comes despite closer ties between the administration and tech leaders, who are lobbying for lighter AI regulation. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella was among the executives at a White House AI summit on Sep 29.

UNIVERSITIES UNDER SCRUTINY The nine universities also include Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Vance accused them of using J-1 exchange-visitor visas to bring in international students and undercut American wages. Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served. "We will investigate whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research," D'Esposito said. "If an American university is breaking the law to save $1 while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It's institutional betrayal." The probe adds to the administration's long-running fight with Harvard over foreign students. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed Harvard for documents on alleged misconduct by international students and its compliance with federal immigration law. Harvard called that subpoena "unfounded retribution" but said it would comply as far as the law requires.

MANILA, Oct 8 : Asian countries are racing to raise their oil stockpiling capacity, complete a regional power grid and speed up renewables in response to supply risks laid bare by the Iran war. Southeast Asia has been worst hit by the energy impact as 80 per cent of the oil transported through the Strait of Hormuz from the Gulf flowed to the region before the Iran war began. "The most advanced efforts are support for the development of oil stockpiling systems in each country and regional joint stockpiling on (a) voluntary basis," nine Southeast Asian nations said in a joint statement issued along with Japan and Australia.  Japan agreed on action plans with its Asian partners to boost crude oil reserves across the region following a meeting of the Japan-led Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC), a Japanese state minister on trade said on Thursday.

After a separate session with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, Japan's State Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Takagi Kei said they had expressed a willingness to cooperate to strengthen Asia's oil stockpiling capacity. Philippines, which imports nearly all of its oil and fuel, will create a national reserve by the end of 2027, its energy secretary, Sharon Garin said on Thursday, adding that it could subsequently be converted into a regional stockpile. The Southeast Asian archipelago is the chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) this year. Garin said countries will decide if they want to host a regional oil stockpile, and also the terms of sale that should be determined by the country itself.  "In the Philippines, what we want is if there's any country that wants to store the crude or their petroleum products here. In case of any emergency the country gets priority on this on the stocks," she said. The ASEAN member countries also pledged to increase the share of clean energy in power generation, targeting 30 per cent renewables in total primary energy supply and 45 per cent in installed power capacity. The region is among the biggest laggards in green energy. Renewables make up 14.1 per cent of primary energy, well short of a 2025 target of 25 per cent, while green power has made up 33.7 per cent of total capacity since 2020 against a 2025 target of 35 per cent, the ninth ASEAN energy outlook showed this week. The countries also reached an enhanced preliminary agreement on developing a long-delayed regional power grid, which Garin called a landmark accomplishment. The concept of a regional electricity network was first announced in December 1997.   "The first study was to connect with 2045, and that's too far because that's 20 years. So they're reviewing again to make it a faster implementation," Garin said.

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 8 : Amazon on Thursday unveiled a slate of higher-end tablets that for the first time feature its Alexa+ voice assistant and run on Google's Android operating system, a bet that consumers will pay more for premium devices after years of focusing on the budget end of the market. Seattle-based Amazon had been working on the tablets under the code name Kittyhawk, as Reuters reported exclusively last year, to transition away from its more limited homegrown Fire OS operating system software, after years of gripes from consumers and app developers. Fire OS is a “forked” version of Android, with modifications to make it work like a unique operating system. Known as Alexa Tablets, the line features several different versions with starting prices from $230 to $500; all are made with aluminum cases, a switch from Fire tablets’ plastic. The new tablets will cost as much as $550, a big bump from Amazon’s more recent top-of-the-line Fire HD 10 tablet which cost upwards of $180, though the company often discounted them.

The top Alexa tablet, with 128 gigabytes of memory, for $550 compares with an Apple iPad for $450 and Samsung's Galaxy tablet for $550. The product revamp marks a new strategy under devices chief Panos Panay to move upscale and away from the inexpensive gadgets Amazon sold at or near cost to hook customers into using Prime Video, Kindle, music apps and the main e-commerce website. That focus on affordability came with compromises, like lower screen quality and battery life, compared with rivals Apple and Samsung and others. Alexa+, an advanced AI-powered version of the Alexa voice assistant, will feature prominently on the devices to help perform actions or answer questions using generative AI. Accessing Alexa+ on the tablets will require a Prime membership or Alexa+ subscription, Amazon said. Amazon is pushing the pricier devices as worldwide tablet sales are falling, down 12 per cent in the second quarter from the year before to 33.6 million units, according to IDC data. The US market, which has been especially hurt by a shortage of memory chips, saw sales plunge 32 per cent in the second quarter year over year, IDC data showed. The Seattle company held just 1.9 per cent of the global tablet market in this year’s second quarter, down from 8 per cent a year earlier, according to IDC. Apple is the leader with 34 per cent, followed by Samsung at 17.5 per cent. The tablet prices do not include a one-time fee customers have to pay to turn off advertising displayed on the lockscreen, though the highest-priced Alexa Tablet will not have the ads. It will require a one-time $20 fee to eliminate the ads, up from $15 for Fire OS tablets, a spokesperson said. Such ads help users “discover new content that’s relevant to their interests” and the revenue helps underwrite other innovations, the spokesperson said. UPGRADE FROM FIRE OS With Android, Alexa Tablet customers won’t be limited to the apps offered in the Fire OS app store, disdained by developers who had to make a third version of apps offered in the Google Play and Apple stores. And the built-in Alexa+ voice AI assistant helps to differentiate the tablets from others. Amazon has spent billions overhauling Alexa to power it with generative AI and make it more capable for connected homes, shopping and accessing third-party services like Uber and Grubhub. The service, free with a Prime membership, is unprofitable. Prior Fire OS tablets will still work, said the spokesperson, but she did not say whether Amazon will continue to maintain the operating system or app store. Earlier this year Amazon cut off support for older Kindle models, citing software maintenance costs as a reason.

AMSTERDAM, Oct 8 : A successor to ASML's most advanced chipmaking machine could be ready in about 10 years, engineers for the company and its optics partner Carl Zeiss said in a peer-reviewed paper. The tool, dubbed "Hyper NA", would print smaller circuitry while re-using much of the companies' existing technology, the paper said, though challenges remain. The machine, which ASML has begun developing but has not committed to producing, matters for the company's future prospects, as well as those of its partners and competitors.  ASML had no immediate comment.

The company is Europe's most valuable by market capitalization, thanks to its monopoly on lithography tools that use extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light to print the tiny circuitry of AI chips. SMALLER, FASTER CHIPS The paper in the October issue of the Journal of Micro/Nanopatterning, Materials and Metrology says Hyper NA could print features as small as 5 nanometers, more than a third smaller than ASML's current "High NA" EUV tool.  Though chipmakers are improving chips with 3-D designs, smaller features remain key for speed and power usage, and lithography is a limiting factor. Among chip manufacturers, Intel has begun using High NA in production, while last month Samsung and SK Hynix said they would follow in 2028 and TSMC in 2030. The paper said Zeiss can already make mirrors precise enough for Hyper NA, and the machine would be barely larger than High NA tools, already the size of a double-decker bus. Beyond Hyper NA, the authors said, tools would likely need to use a shorter wavelength of light, still a matter for academic research.  They said ASML's current light source "can be reused as is" for Hyper NA, while mentioning in a note that an alternative technique with free electron lasers would not change the lighting system's design. Those remarks are relevant for US startups including xLight, which is developing free-electron laser light sources that Elon Musk has hinted he might favor at his Terafab chip plant in Texas, and for Substrate, which is pursuing X-ray lithography.

Oct 8 : Investor concerns that Nvidia-backed Firmus may cut the size of its $5 billion Australian initial public offering (IPO) drove a 30 per cent plunge in shares of construction services provider Maas Group, which owns 3.2 per cent in the AI data centre operator. The final details of Firmus' share sale, the second-largest ever in Australia, were still being finalised on Thursday, according to a person familiar with the matter. Firmus did not respond to a request for comment from Reuters. Sentiment towards AI has shifted sharply in recent weeks as concerns over high valuations have broadened to worries the technology is slipping out of human control and the prospect that massive technology spending may never pay off.

Firmus and its advisors on Thursday were contemplating cutting the size of the IPO and reducing the price per share from A$11 each to A$8.25, according to local media reports. Bookbuilding closed earlier Thursday and potential investors were told in a term sheet reviewed by Reuters "the joint active bookrunners will provide further information in relation to the offer." SOME INVESTORS SAY THEY ARE WARY OF VALUATION The deal's initial term sheet had said indicative offers for the IPO were already above the deal's size. But some potential investors told Reuters they were cautious about the company's burgeoning valuation, ability to execute on its ambitious growth plans and hefty debt pile. Demand for Firmus stock from overseas investors was weaker than expected for the IPO, the reports said, which was to be a landmark transaction for Australia's subdued capital markets. Shares of Maas closed down 22.4 per cent on Thurday, after falling much as 30 per cent in intraday trading, its weakest level since May 6. The company lost about A$517 million ($359.52 million) in market. It is valued at A$1.79 billion. Maas was questioned by the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) over the share price plunge. The company said in an exchange filing that speculation over whether the IPO would proceed had weighed on sentiment, adding it was not aware of any undisclosed information that would explain the trading "The selloff reflects a legitimate derating of the embedded value of its Firmus stake, but the magnitude is overdone," said Emanuel Ajay Datt, managing director of fund manager Datt Group. A cut in Firmus' offer price to A$9 from A$11 would reduce the value of Maas' holding by about A$75 million, Datt said, adding that the loss was modest relative to the company's market value decline on the day. Firmus' $5 billion IPO was to be Australia's largest new share sale in nearly three decades, behind only top telco Telstra's roughly $10 billion float in 1997. ($1 = 1.4380 Australian dollars)

Source: Reuters

Oct 8 : Technology companies and utilities are increasingly exploring ways to make power-hungry data centers more flexible in when and how they consume electricity, helping ease the strain on US power grids as AI-driven demand surges. The strategy, called "demand response", involves data centers temporarily reducing or shifting electricity use during periods of peak demand or grid stress, and is gaining traction as a way to reduce the need for costly grid upgrades and new power generation. It's a tool that states around the US, federal agencies and market operators are increasingly exploring, said Lauren Shwisberg, a principal at energy think tank RMI. WHY DOES DATA CENTER FLEXIBILITY MATTER?

US data center electricity use could rise from about 177 to 192 terawatt-hours in 2024 to between 383 and 793 TWh by 2030, according to the Electric Power Research Institute. Meanwhile, data centers surveyed by the group reported peak power reduction potential of 10 per cent to 30 per cent, depending on facility type, with some hyperscalers going even higher, according to Arin Kaye, EPRI technical leader. A study by Duke University's Nicholas Institute estimated that greater flexibility from data centers could save between $40 billion and $150 billion in capital investments over the next decade. It could also help data centers connect to the grid more quickly, as regulators and grid operators explore faster pathways for facilities willing to curb electricity use during periods of high demand. WHERE DO EFFORTS STAND? So far, the "demand response" strategy for data centers has mostly been deployed through pilot projects or one-off agreements. OpenAI, for example, recently agreed to cut the electricity it draws from the grid by up to 1 gigawatt from a planned 3.2-gigawatt facility in Georgia during periods of grid stress. This, however, is gradually evolving into a broader push. Federal regulators in June ordered grid operators to consider new rules for connecting large power users to the grid, including new pathways for facilities offering this flexibility to connect faster. Last month, Alphabet's Google, NVIDIA and Emerald AI launched an initiative called the AI Energy Management Alliance, aimed at advancing the deployment of "flexible" data centers. WHAT ARE THE KEY CHALLENGES? Experts say scaling up the strategy will require changes on both sides. Data centers need to figure out how to adjust power consumption without disrupting customers, while utilities and grid operators need to develop tariffs, market incentives and faster interconnection pathways that reward that flexibility. "Demand response can materially soften peak impacts, but scaling curtailment agreements across hundreds of new facilities will demand significant capital expenditure and coordinated policy frameworks," said Alexander Kheder, analyst with BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions.

Source: Reuters
